Chair of the Evaluation Committee

Dear Members of the Evaluation Committee,

Please find enclosed my application for promotion from Associate Professor to Full Professor in the Department of Computer Science. I was promoted to Associate Professor at Bishop’s in July 2026, and I submit this application at the Committee’s invitation, for the current cycle. Before joining Bishop’s, I served for six years as Assistant and then Associate Professor at Sultan Qaboos University (SQU), Oman (2017–2023). In accordance with Article 7.06 g) of the Faculty Collective Agreement, I respectfully ask that my research, teaching and service from those six years be included in the assessment. The supporting evidence is attached in the appendices.

Teaching is central to my work. At Bishop's I have taught and developed courses spanning programming, databases, artificial intelligence, neural networks, data visualization, and natural language processing, at both the undergraduate and graduate levels. The 2026 Excellence in Teaching Award at Bishop's (Appendix B4) recognizes this work; my earlier teaching at SQU included full curriculum development for a new MSc in Data Science and recognition as Distinguished Academician (Best Teacher), College of Science, for 2020–2021 (Appendix B4).

My research asks how useful, interpretable structure can be learned from complex data, particularly when labels are scarce. It connects matrix factorization, manifold learning, and meta-unsupervised learning with applications in medical data analysis, remote sensing, and most recently privacy-preserving federated learning. My 38 journal articles and 36 refereed conference papers include work in Pattern Recognition, IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing, Knowledge-Based Systems, and Expert Systems with Applications. This program is currently supported by an NSERC Discovery Development Grant, a Mitacs Accelerate award, a CFI John R. Evans Leaders Fund award as co-PI, and three Bishop's Research and Creative Activity Grants.

Graduate and undergraduate supervision connects this research to student development. My record includes postdoctoral, doctoral, master’s and undergraduate supervision across institutions in Canada, Oman, Algeria and Qatar. My students have won two Best Conference Student Paper Awards in 2025 at Bishop’s, and at Sultan Qaboos University a Best Supervised MSc Thesis award (2020) and two Best Published Paper awards (2023 and 2024). My role as Head of the AI Track at AMI-Lab and my 2026 adjunct appointments at the Université de Sherbrooke and UQO extend the collaborative environment available for this training.

I have also contributed through departmental leadership, University committees, scholarly assessment, conference organization, and outreach. At Bishop’s, this includes serving as Interim Chair in Fall 2024, membership of the Task Force on Generative AI, and representation on the Senate Teaching and Learning Centre Initiative Committee. At Sultan Qaboos University (2017–2023), I chaired the Course Files Committee, the Publicity Committee and two research groups (Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning; Data Science and its Applications), served on the quality assurance and postgraduate studies committees, and held brief Interim Chair responsibilities.

The enclosed narrative, CV, and evidence register set out the basis for my request. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss this dossier and my plans for continued contribution to Bishop's University.

2.1 Teaching philosophy
2.1.1 What I aim to do

My aim is to help students understand why a method works, when it is appropriate, and what its limitations are. In computing and AI, obtaining output is only part of learning: students also need to explain their choices, interpret results, and recognize when a method does not answer the question they are investigating. My teaching ranges from introductory programming, where programming is a practical way to reason about information for students taking computing as part of a broader education, to advanced AI and data analysis, where mathematical understanding, algorithmic reasoning, and careful evaluation matter more.
2.1.2 Why I take this approach

I connect concepts, implementation, and interpretation because students need all three to use computing responsibly: a working program can conceal weak understanding, and an explanation without practical application can leave students unable to use what they have learned. My assessment principles accordingly emphasize reasoning as well as implementation, with clear expectations and opportunities to learn from feedback, which is reflected in the project-based design of CS446, CS307, CS316, and CS504.
2.1.3 Why I consider the approach effective

I consider the approach effective when students can explain a method in their own words, justify their choices, apply it to a new problem, and identify limitations in their results. My 2026 Excellence in Teaching Award and the student research accomplishments in Section 2.2.4 are relevant indicators, but they do not by themselves establish the effect of anyone teaching practice; that connection is substantiated through the evaluation record in Section 2.2.2 and Appendix B1.

A concrete illustration is the Honor’s project on deep learning for object detection, completed in 2025. The student first met this material in CS446 (Intelligent Systems and Neural Networks), Fall 2023, a course I developed around project-based work with real datasets. Their experience in the course motivated them to undertake an Honor’s project in the area, which I supervised through problem formulation, implementation, evaluation, and writing of a neural-network object-detection system. They had no prior experience training neural networks; by the end she had built and evaluated an object-detection model on her own. This is a single example rather than proof of general effect, but it connects the course-level aim in Section 2.1.1, that students understand and justify their methods rather than only run them, to a sustained piece of independent work. She subsequently completed a computer vision and machine learning internship at an autonomous-systems company (USA) and began an MSc at York University. Supporting records are in Appendix B7.1.
2.2 Highlight teaching effectiveness
2.2.1 Preparation and effective course delivery

My Bishop's teaching record spans data visualization, programming for data science, image processing, databases, general computing, introductory AI, and neural networks. I developed CS219 around Python for students from computer science and other disciplines; developed CS446 in intelligent systems and neural networks; and developed CS320 and CS520 around natural language processing and large language models. These contributions support both access to computing and progression into advanced study. The course inventory in Appendix B1 records, for each offering, the course and term and the student evaluation scores, compared with the institutional average at Bishop’s and with the department and college averages at SQU. The resource portfolio in Appendix B2 connects selected syllabi and assessments with the learning outcomes they address.

My lectures follow a consistent structure, which I use in e.g., CS405/CS505. I begin by asking students to recall briefly what we covered in the previous lecture, which refreshes the material and shows me what has stuck. I then present a new problem situation and give students two to three minutes to think about a possible solution. When a student offers a tentative answer, I invite the class to comment on it, so that students practice evaluating reasoning, not only producing answers. Only then do I state the lecture's objectives and outline. From there I formalize the problem mathematically and introduce the tool best suited to solving it. I also present the main alternatives, explain why I favor the first tool, and discuss the strengths and limitations of each. Finally, I show how the chosen method is implemented algorithmically, followed by a short program that solves the problem, so students see the path from the problem to mathematics to working code. Sometimes when students appear lost, I return to the previous step and re-explain it with a different example before moving on. Some selected slides in Appendix B2 (a selection, not the complete set) illustrate the structure described above of my cross-listed course CS405/CS505 given in Fall 2026 are shown in Appendix B2.

3. Research and scholarship
3.1 Research vision and development
3.1.1 A continuing question across different applications

The central question in my research is how to learn useful and interpretable structure from complex data. My early work addressed this through image segmentation, document restoration, and multispectral analysis; later work extended it to remote sensing, matrix factorization, clustering, manifold learning, and medical data analysis. My recent work on meta-unsupervised and federated learning addresses how learning methods can adapt across tasks and data settings. These topics are connected by a shared interest in representations: what information a method preserves, how that information supports learning, and whether a user can interpret the resulting structure.
3.1.2 Three linked directions

The first direction concerns representation and unsupervised learning, including nonnegative matrix factorization, clustering, dimensionality reduction, and meta-unsupervised learning. The second concerns learning from complex observations, including images, multimodal signals, and graph representations. The third concerns the conditions under which learning is useful in practice: limited labels, anomaly detection, medical interpretation, and privacy-preserving collaboration.

3.2. Research trajectory: from data representation to federated meta-unsupervised learning

My research has followed one question: how can a machine learn useful structures from data when labels are few and the data is spread across places that cannot share it? Each stage below leads to the next.
3.2.1 Representation and structure (2013–2021)

My early work studied how the way an image is represented affects what can be recovered from it: historical document restoration (Pattern Recognition, 2013; J36) and color-to-gray conversion (IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, 2015; J35). I also shared resources for other researchers (SMADI, LC2G, and the multispectral text extraction competition at ICDAR 2015). I then moved to non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). My paper, “NMF with feature relationship preservation penalty term for clustering problems” (Pattern Recognition, 2021; J20), shows that a representation must keep the structure of the data if it is to be useful for learning. This idea is the basis of my later work. This work won the IEEE Oman Section Best Paper Award (IEEE Region 8) in 2021. Appendix C3.
3.2.2 Learning with few labels, and on medical data

Next, I worked on learning when labelled examples are scarce. Examples are change detection in remote sensing (IEEE TGRS, 2016; J34, IEEE JSTARS, 2020; J26). I applied the same ideas to medical data with collaborators: histopathology images, Alzheimer’s-related modelling, sleep-stage analysis (J01, J08), seizure detection (C04, C01) and medical report summarization (C02). Two lessons from this work shaped my current program. Medical data has few labels. And it is sensitive, so it often cannot be pooled in one place.
3.2.3 Meta-unsupervised learning (2025)

I then asked how representation learning can work across many tasks instead of one. With my MSc student A. Khan, M. Allaoui and G. Zhong, I published “Meta-Unsupervised Representation Learning: A New Approach to Factorization and Interpretability” (Canadian AI, 2025; C10). It grew from a completed master’s project at Bishop’s. In parallel, my work on manifold learning and visualization (J10, J09, J07, J05) and on graph and anomaly methods (AISTATS 2026, C06; UAI 2026, C03) extends representation learning to embeddings, distributions and graphs.
3.2.4 Federated meta-unsupervised learning: the emerging program

My current program joins the two threads above: learning across tasks (meta-unsupervised learning) and learning across separate data holders without sharing their data (federated learning). The aim is privacy-preserving federated AI for healthcare, where data stays at each hospital or site. Early outputs are the preprint “FIRMA: FIbonacci Ring Model Aggregation for Privacy-preserving Federated Learning” (arXiv, 2026; PP01) and a submitted patent disclosure, Fed-Z-NMF (P01). They are not peer-reviewed publications or granted patents. The program is supported by my NSERC Discovery Development Grant, CFI / Mitacs / Research and Creative Activity Grants (Section 3.5), and it trains graduate students at Bishop’s (Appendix D).

6. Future contribution
6.1 Priorities for the next stage

My next stage of work will deepen the connection between teaching, research, and student development. The priorities below are proposed directions; their scale will depend on student demand, available resources, approvals, and successful funding applications.
6.1.1 Teaching and student projects

I plan to develop a clearer progression from foundational computing and AI courses to supervised projects with a manageable scope, a clear question, appropriate data, and assessment that requires students to explain their reasoning. I also plan to strengthen my evidence of teaching effectiveness. I will document course revisions, review student feedback in context, and collect examples of assessed learning, including a documented response to the CS462/562 evaluation result noted in Section 2.2.2. I have developed the Natural Language Processing (CS320) and Large Language Models (CS520) courses I’m teaching for the first time in Fall 2026. I will revise them after their first offerings, using student feedback and assessment results if needed.
6.1.2 Research and supervision

My research priorities are to consolidate the meta-unsupervised learning program, develop work on representations and anomaly detection, and investigate privacy-preserving learning for distributed data. Medical and physiological data remain an important application direction through existing collaborations. For supervision, I plan to use clearly defined milestones, realistic project scope, and explicit contribution records, while seeking opportunities for students to present, publish, and collaborate.
6.1.3 Institutional contribution and collaboration

I intend to support interdisciplinary projects where computing expertise can help colleagues investigate a substantive question, and to help translate such problems into feasible student projects. Establishing BRAIN as a recognized research center, through a formal Senate proposal, is a near-term priority that would consolidate AI research capacity and graduate training at Bishop's.

COURSE SYLLABUS
CS 320 — Natural Language Processing (NLP)
1. Course Description

Language is the primary medium through which humans communicate, reason, and record knowledge. Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the subfield of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence concerned with enabling computers to understand, process, and generate human language. From search engines and spam filters to machine translation and intelligent assistants, NLP underlies a broad range of technologies that shape modern business and daily life.

CS320 provides a rigorous yet accessible introduction to the core concepts, algorithms, and practical tools of NLP. The course is designed for a mixed audience of Computer Science (BSc CS) and Business/Information Technology (BSc BAIT) students at the third-year undergraduate level. Mathematical content is presented at a moderate level: formal notation is used where appropriate, but every formula is accompanied by a plain-language explanation, and no result is expected to be derived from first principles. The emphasis is on conceptual understanding and practical application.

The course follows the classical NLP pipeline — from raw text to intelligent applications — progressing from statistical foundations through neural sequence models. It stops deliberately before the Transformer architecture, which is the entry point of CS 520 level (Large Language Models). Students who complete CS320 will have the background necessary to understand and critically evaluate modern language technology, including the limitations and ethical concerns it raises.

This course covers: text preprocessing, statistical language models, vector space representations, word embeddings, text classification, sequence labeling, syntactic parsing, recurrent neural networks, the encoder-decoder framework with attention, and NLP ethics.
This course does not cover (reserved for CS 520): Transformer architectures, BERT, GPT and other large language models, fine-tuning, prompt engineering, and retrieval-augmented generation.
2. Learning Outcomes
Upon successful completion of CS320, students will be able to:
Knowledge and Understanding
Explain the main challenges of NLP and the role of the different levels of linguistic analysis.
Describe statistical n-gram language models and the need for smoothing.
Distinguish sparse and dense text representations and justify their use.
Explain the evolution from RNNs/LSTMs to attention-based models.
Skills and Application
Build a complete text preprocessing pipeline using Python, NLTK and/or spaCy.
Implement and evaluate classical text classifiers on real datasets.
Apply pre-trained word embeddings for similarity and analogy tasks.
Design, implement and present a small NLP project.
Professional and Ethical Awareness
Identify sources of bias in NLP systems and discuss ethical and regulatory considerations (including relevant Canadian frameworks).

6. Course Policies
6.1 Academic Integrity

All work submitted for evaluation must be the student's own. Collaboration is encouraged for conceptual understanding, but all code, written analyses, and reports must be produced independently, unless explicit pair work is authorized.

Use of generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot) must be disclosed in any submission. Undisclosed use of AI-generated content constitutes academic dishonesty under the Bishop's University Academic Integrity Policy. Students are responsible for familiarizing themselves with that policy.
Plagiarism detection software may be used to verify originality. Suspected violations will be reported to the Academic Integrity Committee.
6.2 Accessibility and Accommodation

Bishop's University is committed to providing equitable access to education for all students. Students with documented disabilities or other circumstances requiring accommodation should contact the SAS Office and provide official documentation. Students are encouraged to notify the instructor of their accommodation plan within the first two weeks of the term so that appropriate arrangements can be made in a timely manner.
6.3 Attendance

Regular attendance at lectures sessions is expected. Lecture slides and any supplementary materials will be posted on Moodle; however, in-class discussion, worked examples, and live coding demonstrations are integral parts of the learning experience and will not be recorded. Students who miss a class are responsible for obtaining notes from a classmate and reviewing posted materials.
6.4 Communication and Office Hours

The instructor will respond to email enquiries within two business days. For questions of general interest, students are strongly encouraged to use the course discussion forum on Moodle; answers provided there benefit all students. Office hours will be posted on Moodle at the beginning of the term. Students requiring assistance outside of office hours may arrange an appointment by email.
6.5 Inclusive Learning Environment

This course is designed to be accessible to both Computer Science and BAIT students. Each group brings different strengths: CS students may have stronger programming and mathematical foundations, while BAIT students may have stronger domain knowledge in business applications of technology. These differences are a resource, not a barrier. Questions are always welcome, and no level of question is considered too basic. Students are expected to treat their peers with respect and professionalism.
7. Required Tools and Resources
All software used in this course is freely available. A detailed installation guide and a configuration-verification notebook will be distributed via Moodle in the first week.

Students who encounter difficulty installing the software locally may use Google Colaboratory (https://colab.research.google.com), a free cloud-based Jupyter environment that requires only a Google account. All assignment notebooks are tested to run on both local installations and Google Colab.
7.2 Course Platform
All course materials — slides, assignment notebooks, announcements, grades, and the discussion forum — are hosted on Bishop's University Moodle. Students must check Moodle regularly.

This syllabus is subject to revision. Any modifications will be announced on Moodle with a minimum of one week's notice. The instructor reserves the right to adjust the pace and content of individual lectures to better serve the learning needs of the class.
